i'm the reporter. mr president, last december our parliament ratified the protocol of accession of ecuador to the 2013 free trade agreement between the european union, colombia and peru. ecuador, the world's largest producer of bananas and the largest exporter to the union, will now benefit from a significant reduction in customs duties on its exports to the union. this is obviously a game changer and may eventually destabilise the european banana sector. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. it is the source of some 37 000 jobs. it should also be noted that bananas are included in the european list of so-called "sensitive" agricultural products and that they meet high standards of sustainability in social, environmental and health matters, standards that are not applied in the latin american production chain. in this context, it is therefore very important that european banana producers be better protected. i am therefore very pleased that the position of our parliament has been heard and taken into account by the commission and the council. i would like to thank in particular our commissioner, cecilia malmström. i would also like to thank the chairman of our inta committee, the non-attached rapporteurs and the colleagues who have been very involved in this matter. thanks to all of you, we have a text which is a substantial step forward and which provides practical answers to safeguard our sector. now, not only will producers be better informed, but they will also be more involved in monitoring market developments. the commission will have to carry out an annual and in-depth study of the situation on the european banana market and of european producers, including after the expiry of the mechanism. it will also involve member states and stakeholders, allowing them to exchange information on developments on the european banana market in ad hoc meetings. this is important and it directly meets a major demand from producers. this will allow for a regular dialogue between stakeholders and the commission and address all producer concerns, such as the evolution of volumes and the impact of imports on prices and european production. the commission will also need to improve its statistical databases to allow much more detailed and regular monitoring of the situation on the european banana market and to make these data more accessible. finally, and this is very important, an early warning mechanism is created when 80% of the trigger volume of the stabilisation mechanism is reached by one of the countries covered by the mechanism. the commission will now have a legal obligation to inform parliament and the council in writing. it will also have to provide all statistical data and import volumes for the other eight countries covered, so that stakeholders can have a general overview of the situation and better forecast future overruns. if the thresholds are found to be exceeded by one of the countries covered by the mechanism, the commission will have a legal obligation to act, either by temporarily suspending the preferential duties or by demonstrating that such a taxation is not required. the commission will be required to carry out a full evaluation of the functioning of the mechanism by 1 january 2019, one year before its expiry. if, following this assessment, the commission considers that the situation of producers has deteriorated, it shall extend the period of validity of the mechanism after agreement of the stakeholders. the commission will also have to continue to carry out annual analyses of the market situation, of the situation of producers after 2020, and to take action in the event of a deterioration in production. all these changes will apply to peru, colombia, ecuador, but also to the central american countries which are parties to the association agreement with the european union. our parliament regions which are so important for our europe.

minds of everyone these days: the future of our union. the commission welcomes the initiatives of the european parliament to boldly look forward. this is something that our president, jean-claude juncker, has been promoting since the beginning of our mandate. we have closely followed the reports drawn up by ms bresso, mr brok and mr verhofstadt, and also the related reports on the eurozone of which could be the topic of a separate debate. i will therefore not attempt to comment on the details. my president is currently preparing a white paper on the future of europe in the run-up to the rome summit in march. we therefore appreciate very much the many interesting viewpoints and proposals set out in these proposals, which provide useful information and also inspiration. the bresso-brok report rightly points to the significant, untapped potential within the existing framework, such as further reform to the institutional structure of economic and monetary union. the verhofstadt report by the members this morning. with regard to the böge-berès report, it was only adopted last night in committee, but let me say this: our common goal is a more resilient and prosperous economic and the agenda calls for the debate on the report by monica macovei, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the strengthening of checks in databases relevant to external borders (com ((2015) 0670 - c8-0407/2015 - 2015/0307 ((cod)) (a8-0218/2016).
member of the commission. – madam president, in the wake of the terrorist attacks in paris, the commission proposed the amendment to the schengen borders code introducing systematic checks for all citizens at our external borders. as we have just heard, these checks are vital to stopping, amongst others, potential terrorists, not just from coming into the eu, but also to prevent them from travelling to conflict zones. on behalf of my colleague, commissioner avramopoulos, as well as myself, i would like to say how grateful we are to the parliament, and in particular to the rapporteur, mrs macovei, for the work that they have done on this important dossier. the amendment will oblige member states to carry out systematic checks on all persons crossing an external border. they will be checked – as mrs macovei has just set out – against law enforcement databases, notably the schengen information system, to verify that they do not pose a threat to public order or internal security. this obligation will apply at all external borders – air, sea and land – both at entry and exit. however, if a systematic consultation of databases leads to a disproportionate impact on the flow of border traffic, then member states will have the option of carrying out targeted checks against the databases, provided that they first carry out an appropriate risk assessment. in the case of airports – again, as we have just heard – this option is generally only available for a transition arrangement of six months unless an airport has specific infrastructure problems, in which case an exception can be made to extend that transition period up to 18 months. the eu will provide financial assistance to member states to help them implement the new rules and in turn – like others here – i trust that the member states will do their utmost to be ready on time and that the new measures will translate into immediate and tangible results. the amended schengen borders code, together with the european border and coast guards, are crucial in our bid to preserve freedom of movement within the schengen area and to ensure the security of our citizens. we now need to press ahead with work on reinforcing the management and security of the eu’s external borders, including the work on the entry—exit and etias proposals. this is all part of returning to a fully functioning schengen area from which all our citizens benefit.
the committee on foreign affairs has tabled a number of amendments. madam president, from now on, checks at all the eu's external land, sea and air borders will be compulsory for all eu citizens and for all third country nationals. this revision of the schengen borders code is a direct response to the terrorist attacks on european soil and, in particular, i cannot forget, in paris. this amendment will make it possible to introduce systematic checks on persons entering and leaving the european territory, as well as systematic checks in databases. this decision can restore credibility to schengen, provided it is implemented quickly and effectively at all our borders and accompanied by the effective establishment of european coastguards and border guards. all the major countries in the world have effective controls at their external borders, and it is time for the european union to do the same for the security and protection of our citizens.
for the gue/ngl group madam president, my group is firmly opposed to this amendment to the schengen regulation, which is supposed to establish systematic and compulsory border checks. it is a new stage in the construction of a safe fortress europe, which has taken a new turn since 2015 in the name of the fight against terrorism and the so-called migration crisis, confusing the one with the other and in fact fuelling racism and xenophobia. the member states subscribe to this structure, which allows them to shoulder their responsibilities on the back of the european union. this regulation cannot be seen in isolation from the other texts currently before us, in particular the misnamed 'smart borders'. this text will make it possible to control third-country nationals on their entry and, from now on, on their exit and, to make things right, european citizens are added to it. in practice, however, checks will be random, and the relevant databases will only be consulted if there is any doubt about the validity of the travel documents. member states will be able to suspend compulsory checks to smooth traffic. i'm surprised at you. and certain categories of people may also be exempted. so, in the end, this device is really variable geometry. i see in reality a great deal of hypocrisy, if not cynicism, at the expense of fundamental rights, without the right to security and, above all, the right to security of our fellow citizens being strengthened.
madam president, in view of the current state of threats, i can only stress the need to better manage our common external borders and to ensure freedom of movement for all within the schengen area. it is only then that it will function normally again, and that is our aim, because returning to national borders is not an option. however, two points are necessary here. firstly, the socialist group will remain vigilant about the accumulation of checks, audits and databases. our efforts to keep our citizens safe could be counterproductive. secondly, i will be attentive to the practical implementation of these measures by the member states, in particular the need for airports to adapt their infrastructures for the application of systematic checks. i do not want the situation with the npr directive to happen again. the council also pressed parliament to adopt the text quickly, whereas today it is clear that only four member states are on the verge of having an operational pnr. safety is everyone's business. it is only through better cooperation between all actors, both european and national, that we can effectively respond to the threats we face today.

on behalf of the enf group. mr president, intelligent robots have become a reality. they are machines programmed to make decisions, like, for example, driverless cars or certain surgical robots. the delvaux report is right to be concerned about them, because their intelligence will, in the near future, exceed the intellectual capacities of human beings. the use of such services must therefore be governed by ethical principles, such as respect for privacy and human freedom. the delvaux report, unfortunately, advocates dangerous solutions in terms of liability, because it does not simply recommend the introduction of a compulsory insurance scheme and a guarantee fund, as it should have done. it envisages the creation of a specific legal personality for robots, which would be tantamount to considering robots as 'responsible electronic persons'. i object to this prospect for two reasons: firstly, because it would absolve their manufacturers and users of all liability, which would undoubtedly please powerful lobbies; and secondly, and above all, because i believe, as does jacques maritain, that the human person has a spiritual super-existence to which no artificial intelligence can be compared.

in writing. this debate on the decriminalization of domestic violence in russia is symptomatic of the continuing misinformation about the state in the western media. under the revised article 116 of the russian criminal code, domestic or family violence without health consequences will now be punishable by 15 days of administrative detention, a fine of 30,000 rubles or 180 hours of community service. this reform removes a legal inconsistency. in fact, perpetrators of violence without consequences on health (such as spanking, in relation to children) were previously subject to criminal law on the pretext of their status as 'close relatives' of the complainant. violence of similar gravity, which any other individual would have been guilty of, fell under the civil law. domestic violence that causes harm to health, even if it is harmless, remains a criminal offence and carries a penalty of up to two years' imprisonment. the reform also introduced the restrictive orders, which were unknown in russian law until then. russian society is as opposed to domestic violence as western european societies. the reform is simply intended to prevent any interference by the state in the family sphere.

on behalf of the ppe group. mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to thank my colleagues in the parliament, the commission and the council with whom i have worked closely to improve the protection of european citizens against the harmful effects of mercury. as rapporteur for the epp group, i welcome the results of these negotiations. the text which has finally been submitted to us seems to me to be more realistic than the previous versions. this new text is ambitious to say the least. it puts our europe at the forefront of the fight against heavy metal pollution on the international stage, but it also gives our companies and researchers the time they need to develop viable alternatives. among the main elements of the reform, i would note that the export of mercury is now prohibited and the use of recycled mercury is encouraged. as regards dental amalgam, only encapsulated forms are authorised, ensuring both the health of the patient and the health of the practitioners. dentists will also need to equip themselves with amalgam separators to prevent any release into the environment. for at-risk populations, children, pregnant women, the use of amalgams is prohibited unless otherwise advised by a physician. the agreement also provides for a reduction in mercury levels in products and processes. as regards the management of mercury waste, i have fought with my epp colleagues for the safest storage, i.e. after the waste has been stabilised. in the face of heavy metal pollution, the 'mercury' regulation before us today is an example of an efficient europe that protects. the european union is not a mere institution. i hope that the union will defend its ambitious objectives with vigour at the minamata international convention conference in geneva next september.

in writing. in a survey carried out in the summer of 2014 in 16 rabbit farms in five member states, ongi ciwf france highlighted the dire living conditions of the 340 million rabbits raised in the european union. confined to a4-sized fenced cages, which generate intense stress for the animal, rabbits are the farm animals most exposed to antibiotics. the text under discussion is therefore aimed at the gradual abandonment of battery farming. it removes a legal vacuum: rabbit farming is governed by directive 98/58/ec of 20 july 1998, but is not the subject of any specific text, unlike pigs, calves, laying hens or broilers. i welcome the fact that the material situation of farmers has been taken into account. under the terms of the text, financial support may be granted to them from the european funds under the rural development strand in order to facilitate the transition to a new mode of livestock farming, replacing, in particular, battery farming with enclosed livestock farming. the commission will, in particular, have to promote the consumption of rabbit meat, of which the european union is the second largest producer in the world.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, today i am here speaking on behalf of high representative mogherini as she could not be in the chamber for this debate. however, allow me to remark that the high representative appreciates the work of mr gahler and mr gonzález pons on the report, and her views and those of parliament coincide in many areas. the report addresses critical issues that you have been working on during the implementation of the security and defence aspects of the eu global strategy (eugs). the conclusions reached on the eugs implementation define common strategic priorities and a common vision in security and defence and has set out how csdp, as part of wider eu efforts, can contribute to tackling today’s and tomorrow’s multifaceted security challenges and protect european citizens. i know that high representative mogherini would like to underline, at the very beginning, that she attaches critical importance to working together with the european parliament on defence issues as natural allies in this effort. as you know, on 6 march, high representative mogherini presented the progress achieved in the security and defence implementation of the eugs to the foreign affairs council. the council conclusions adopted served as the first progress report to the march european council according to the tasking received in december last year. on 9 march, the heads of state and government welcomed the work done and asked to continue with even greater determination and speed. the high representative is pleased to report that, despite very tight timelines, significant progress has been made since december. currently there is work being done on the three pillars of the package: not only on the global strategic implementation of security and defence, but also on the european defence action plan from the commission, eu-nato cooperation and the follow-up to the warsaw joint declaration. this work is even more important at a time when expectations and questions are raised more or less openly inside the european union, as well as outside, about the eu’s commitment and ability to act as a security provider. there is no better answer to such expectations and questions than real, tangible progress on concrete issues. on military planning and conduct capability, the foreign affairs council last week agreed to establish a permanent military planning and conduct capability for the european union’s non-executive military missions. it will be established within the european military staff (eums) and will operate under the responsibility and command of the director-general of the military staff. at present, there are three such missions: in mali, central african republic and somalia, which are currently only led by headquarters in the field. this decision will also contribute to enhanced civilian or military cooperation. experts from the military planning and conduct capability (mpcc) and its civilian counterpart, the cpcc, will form a joint support coordination cell to facilitate mutual assistance and coordination. the new structure will be operational in the coming weeks. on defence cooperation: the european external action service also has a clear mandate from the european council to strengthen defence cooperation. ambitions need to be underpinned by sufficient resources, both nationally and at eu level. it is equally important to make more effective use of the defence budgets by reducing fragmentations. the 28 member states, for example, have 154 weapons systems in use. the united states has only 27. moreover, around 80% of defence investment in europe is still spent on a national basis. in the report, reference is also made to the costs of non-european defence. the european defence agency is working hard to strengthen defence cooperation, and the commission is also mobilising its instruments. it is clear that defence capabilities will remain member state-owned. progress in this field, through eu instruments, will also benefit nato, as there will be a single set of forces. therefore, these efforts will be pursued further in a way that ensures coherence with parallel work within nato. it is important to note as well that any success will have an impact on transatlantic burden-sharing. but let us be clear: europeans have to do this for themselves. this is about protecting our citizens. the main current efforts to deepen defence cooperation in developing capabilities are centred on the coordinated annual review on defence, permanent structured cooperation, as well as the european defence action plan. the coordinated annual review on defence should be a member states-driven mechanism. it will contribute to the increased transparency of national defence plans and help make cooperation the norm. based on member states’ guidance, a set of concrete modalities will be prepared. the council has also been tasked with further work on the permanent structured cooperation, an important tool also highlighted in your report. permanent structured cooperation is about enabling those member states who are willing to undertake more binding commitments towards one another to do so. countries wishing to be part of it will need to make concrete commitments and join concrete cooperation projects. while it is open to all member states and maximum inclusiveness is pursued, there is no automaticity or a free ride. permanent structured cooperation can help develop defence capabilities but also to pool and share existing military assets so that we can make more efficient use of them in our operations. member states will work on the common commitments as well as the projects and initiatives they can provide to the permanent structured cooperation. these projects need to be ambitious and support the overarching aim of preparing the most demanding missions. on the european defence action plan, it proposes actions to support member states’ efforts in delivering capabilities through greater cooperation and fostering a strong, competitive and innovative european defence industrial base, including by setting up a european defence fund. these are very important initiatives that also show the added value of the european union to enhance the effectiveness and the performance of our defence sector. once again, on behalf of high representative mogherini, i would like to reiterate that further work on the eu battle groups will be undertaken, as these are key military assets. yet the european union has never deployed a battle group, despite the fact that it could have been useful on several occasions. this will be referred back to council in may. there is also work to be done to improve situational awareness, reinforcing the structures that sustain these efforts, in particular the intelligence and situation centre (intcen). on the capacity-building and support of security and development, a proactive approach is being promoted to identify concrete projects while supporting a positive outcome on the legislative process including the european parliament. the report also highlights the importance of providing appropriate equipment to the forces that the eu trains. it is important to work together across the nexus security or development to achieve peaceful societies protected by armed forces under civilian control.

mr president, it took more than a year of investigation, hearings, and careful consultation of documents to bring this dark matter of dieselgate to light. the conclusions of our inquiry were broadly adopted on 28 february and i welcome that. it shows that with perseverance and good will, in a collective spirit, we always manage to restore the truth beyond appearances, and i thank all those who contributed to this. our conclusions are clear and precise. now we must draw practical conclusions. that is the subject of the resolution adopted today. the european and national institutions have failed, but they now have the opportunity to put things right for the benefit of all, for cleaner air and cities where people can breathe better thanks to cleaner and more controlled cars. the legislation has been misapplied. the commission has therefore to find ways of applying it correctly throughout europe and to strengthen the ex post controls, which remain the best means of combating fraud. what better tool than a specialised european agency to apply the law uniformly, impervious to national interests, with the help of technically qualified experts? other modes of transport in europe, such as air, sea and rail transport, are regulated by agencies. why not road transport? that would be the logical conclusion of our work. the committee of inquiry voted in favour of this last february and jean-claude juncker declared that he was in favour. i hear the arguments, sadly budgetary, that a new agency would be too expensive. i will reply by saying that public health should not be seen as a cost but as an investment, especially when we consider the exorbitant price that europeans pay every year because of air pollution, the thousands of deaths but also the chronic diseases, sometimes of long duration, and the consequences for our health systems. in addition, an agency is not so expensive when it is intelligently set up. for example, it is possible to extend the powers of an existing agency for economies of scale. by building on the work of national authorities but supervising them, such an agency would also save time and money in litigation between two member states. our aim in creating this agency is more europe and, above all, a europe that protects. what we need today is a robust system that ensures compliance with the rules.

on behalf of the enf group. mr president, following the scandals of fraudulently manufactured pip breast implants made from non-medical silicone and metal-metal hip implants which resulted in the spread of highly toxic cobalt, it was decided to scrap the rules on medical devices. unfortunately, these two disputed cases are partly the result of a lack of vigilance by a national health agency. but this does not in any way justify the total loss of the prerogatives of the states as a result of the introduction of the two regulations under discussion today. these new regulations will place unrealistic constraints on notified bodies, which are, by their compulsory approval, the cornerstone of the value chain, as they transfer the competences of the national authorities to these same notified bodies, turning them into a real health police. the consequences are twofold: privatisation of the health system when medical devices are placed on the market and, in addition, a considerable increase in certification costs in return for the liability that will be borne by these bodies and thus their insurance premium in anticipation of future lawsuits. while some provisions are useful, such as improved traceability, the final result is likely to paralyse the european medical device sector rather quickly, particularly the french sector, which is currently unable to support a notified body that is essential. in doing so, these regulations are an unprecedented attack on our health sovereignty. unable to supply their customers, due to the lack of compulsory ce marking, french smes are being forced out of hospitals and pharmacies on the recommendation of the french national agency for the safety of medicines itself, in favour of foreign companies, even outside the european union, albeit with products of lower quality. while these foreign companies also need to obtain the ce marking, their profitability and their prevalence in their home market enable them to withstand the test better, even if, in the long run, the potential lack of auditors will make the european market dependent on imports from third countries. in france, the medical device industry employs about 65 000 people in a thousand companies, of which more than 90% are very small enterprises (mses), with a turnover of 20 billion euros. finally, although this discussion was necessary and expected by the players in the sector, this revision entails a very substantial change in the regulatory requirements extending the certification deadlines. on the contrary, the deadlines for applying these regulations are desirable in the very short term, almost as if by force. for all these reasons, we shall oppose these texts.

member of the commission, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – mr president, honourable members, allow me to stand in for the high representative, vice-president of the commission, ms mogherini, in this very important debate. first of all let me thank you for this report, as well as for your strong support for our work and in particular for the partnership framework approach. the partnership framework approach and your report are based on the same idea: isolation cannot solve the challenges of our time. we need to engage with our partners, build new channels for cooperation with them. and this is particularly true on the issue of migration. i cannot but subscribe to all relevant recommendations in your report. never forget that this is about human beings, so respect for human beings and human rights must come first. work on both short-term fixes and long-term solutions is important. tackle the root causes of irregular migration and forced displacement and work for political and diplomatic solutions to conflicts. engage not only bilaterally but also at the global, regional and local level. this is the cornerstone of our work with third countries on migration. following our debate in february, let me first of all debrief you on our work on the central mediterranean. all services involved, namely the eeas, commission services and council, are working hand in hand together with the presidency and member states on the implementation of the malta summit declaration. it goes without saying that our overall primary objective remains the stabilisation of libya. the terrible situation of migrants trapped in the hands of militias is only one, albeit important, part of the broader difficulties the country is facing. an effective and sustainable long-term response to the migration challenge in the central mediterranean cannot be found without a lasting solution to libya’s governance and security challenges. at the same time we cannot wait for the crisis in libya to be over: too many people risk their lives every day to cross the mediterranean, too many live in terrible conditions inside the country. work is being intensified on all levels as regards more immediate and medium-term migration-related actions. firstly we are stepping up our support for implementing partners, in particular the international organisation for migration and the unhcr. we aim at improving the situation at disembarkation points and inside detention centres. but our cooperation can achieve much also on assisted voluntary returns; according to iom’s analysis, 80% of migrants present in libya are willing to return back to their countries of origin if they are given a safe and dignified opportunity to do so. secondly we have started to facilitate a common approach between libya, chad and niger to better manage libya’s southern borders. the objective is to disrupt the smugglers’ business and provide assistance to migrants who are stranded, vulnerable or willing to return back home, before they embark on hazardous journeys through the desert. thirdly we continue our support to the libyan coastguard through operation sophia and through our seahorse programme in terms of training, to put libya in a condition to manage its territorial waters. last but not least community stabilisation, providing support to libyans as well as migrants, is also an important element under the eu support package for libya. let me in this context highlight the interconnection between our work on various fronts and in particular between our work in libya, the partnership framework approach and the valletta process. as clearly shown in our third progress report on the partnership framework adopted on 2 march, the approach is the right one and needs to be further consolidated. as part of this partnership we are engaging strongly with countries of transit like niger. in parallel we are working with the countries of origin of irregular migration, aiming also at developing cooperation on return and readmission. this is, however, indispensable to address the root causes of the irregular migration flows reaching the european union, and to discourage further migrants from embarking on dangerous journeys through the desert or at sea at the mercy of smugglers and traffickers. in this context it is paramount to ensure the political engagement of our partners to support our work with their own political strategic choices, and with reforms for the prosperity of their countries. in that regard the european external investment plan will be fundamental not only for the major impact that private investments might have for economic development, job creation and growth; the plan also offers the necessary technical assistance to identify and implement reforms for good governance, security and transparency. i do count on this house to continue working speedily towards the final adoption of the investment plan. let me now come back to the partnership framework and share with you the progress achieved with the five priority countries. niger represents a prominent example of successful cooperation on migration. the authorities are engaging proactively in the fight against human smuggling, in particular in the agadez hub. this is crucial as niger is a transit country of migratory flows towards libya. results are there, with a considerable decline of flows through agadez. we need now to stabilise this positive result by enhancing our support to the local communities which are accepting to abandon the smuggling business and expand niger’s model of the fight against migrant smuggling to other countries of transit in the sahel region. this is key also to addressing the possible deviation of the smuggling routes, an issue that we are closely monitoring, including by putting in place a better system of information sharing. our dialogue with mali is on track. we will soon meet with malian authorities to discuss possible areas of cooperation to stem the business of traffickers and smugglers of migrants. these include enhancing mali’s cooperation with neighbouring countries such as niger, which the malian minister for malians abroad visited recently. furthermore the projects we have approved under the eu trust fund for africa will allow iom to deploy activities in several parts of mali to facilitate the voluntary return of migrants transiting mali to their countries and the cooperation with border posts. senegal remains a trusted partner and we see positive developments. the senegalese side has recently taken further steps in the right direction and we expect some concrete results very soon. ethiopia has also adopted a constructive approach in regional and continental dialogues with the european union on migration as current chair of the khartoum process. its contribution, together with mali, was important to the successful outcome of the valletta senior official meeting last february. finally, dialogue and political cooperation with nigeria has been stepped up significantly, although work is still needed with this country which represents the main origin of the irregular migration flows reaching the mediterranean. this challenge we can only manage together and i am glad that our approach, based on migration compacts, has also become the international approach at the last united nations general assembly. the cooperation and experience acquired with the partnership frameworks is something we intend to bring as an eu input in the follow-up to the general assembly during the six informal consultations that are to be held in new york, geneva and vienna.

vice-president of the commission. – mr president, on the subject of globalisation and trade links with beijing, i got back from there only a few hours ago, and if i look tired it is because of the long flight from beijing. today we are discussing the reflection paper on harnessing or shaping globalisation. we are not passive in this regard, but rather an active operator in shaping or harnessing globalisation. this is the second of five planned reflection papers to steer the broad debate on the future of the eu further, following publication of the white paper on 1 march. it takes an honest look at what globalisation has brought to the eu. the fact is that, even if the eu has greatly benefited from globalisation, this means little to our citizens if the benefits are not shared fairly and more evenly. the benefits of globalisation are numerous. people travel, work, learn and live in different countries. they interact with each other on the web, sharing their ideas, cultures and experiences. students have online access to courses run by leading universities across the world. countries can produce more for less by specialising in what they do best and exploiting economies of scale. international competition and scientific cooperation have accelerated innovation. european exports have grown as customers worldwide demand the high—quality goods and services we supply. eighty percent of our exporters are small and medium—sized companies so the beneficiaries of global value chains are those european smes and their workers. actually, eur 1 billion of exports supports 14 000 jobs in the eu. imports are equally important as 80% of them consist of raw materials, capital goods and components necessary for the eu economy to function. globalisation has also helped lift hundreds of millions of people out of poverty and has enabled poorer countries to catch up. but globalisation also brings challenges. the benefits of globalisation are not shared evenly between regions and people. many europeans are concerned that globalisation is leading to inequality, job losses and social injustice or to a lowering of environmental health and privacy standards. for instance, countries with lower wages, environmental standards or taxes have increasingly competed with europe in low-skill and low-value-added segments of industry, leading to factory closures, job losses or downward pressure on our workers’ pay and conditions. some foreign companies and governments have engaged in unfair trade practices, such as dumping, tax evasion or subsidisation, that can lead to overcapacity and unfair advantages. these strategies deprive eu governments of tax revenues and contribute to unfairness. many citizens consider that globalisation and uncontrolled migration directly threaten their identity and way of life. citizens are anxious about not being able to control their own future, let alone the future of their children. these concerns must be recognised and addressed. however, the solution lies neither in isolationism, which has led to disastrous outcomes in the past, nor in laissez-faire politics. the evidence presented in the reflection paper shows clearly that globalisation can be beneficial where it is properly harnessed. the eu must ensure a better distribution of the benefits of globalisation by working together with member states and regions, as well as with international partners and other stakeholders. together we should seize the opportunity to shape globalisation, in line with our own values and interests, in order to respond to its opportunities and challenges. the question is how to do so, and it is vital to have an open and wide-ranging debate about that. the reflection paper offers some ideas in this respect. on the external front, the paper focuses on the need to shape a truly sustainable global order, based on shared values and a common agenda. the eu has always stood for a strong and effective multilateral global rulebook, and it should continue to develop this. for example, the eu could push for new rules and higher standards to create a level playing field by addressing harmful and unfair behaviour such as tax evasion, government subsidies or social dumping. effective trade-defence instruments and better enforcement of domestic and international rules could also help the eu to act decisively against countries or companies that engage in unfair practices. the eu’s progressive trade and investment agreements should continue not only to open markets in a reciprocal way but also to enhance global governance on issues including human rights, working conditions, food safety and environmental protection. on the domestic front, the paper insists on the need to protect and empower citizens through robust social policies and to provide the necessary education and training support throughout their lives. this will equip people for the future and will redistribute wealth more fairly. the paper also underlines the importance of ensuring that europe remains a competitive and innovative economy that will allow it to maintain its leading role in the world. this requires a vision for the future, in order to modernise our economy by embracing digitalisation, technological and social innovations, decarbonisation and the circular economy. it also requires smart specialisation, smart digital, industrial, tax or innovation policies and an improvement in the business environment. the eu cannot achieve all of this by itself. it is a shared responsibility, not only of the eu and the member states but also of regions and municipalities throughout europe. the main word we have to assess carefully is ‘resilience’. what are the policies needed in order to strength the resilience of our people – our citizens – and also our member states?

on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, dear colleagues, honourable members of the european parliament, thank you for taking this timely initiative to discuss the dadaab refugee camp situation. you know the facts. in may 2016 the kenyan government announced its decision to close down the camp in the near future, citing security concerns and the need to end the protracted refugee situation. on 13 november the government announced that the closure would be delayed by six months on humanitarian grounds. according to the announcement, priority was to be given to relocating non-somali refugees to other camps – and this process has started – and to reintegrating kenyans living in the camp. to date over 23 000 refugees have been returned from dadaab to somalia. this year, however, on 9 february, the kenyan high court declared the government’s decision to close the camp null and void and described the repatriation of refugees as unconstitutional and discriminatory. yet the kenyan government has not officially changed its proposed closure date, 31 may 2017. that is 16 days away. the government has recognised that the voluntary repatriation process must be implemented in accordance with the tripartite agreement between kenya, somalia and the unchr. when we consider the situation in dadaab, we must also bear in mind the existing context in the whole of africa, especially in somalia. despite some positive political developments during the past year, a renewed drought is bringing the country to its knees. famine is looming. 6.7 million people, half of the total population, are in need of urgent humanitarian assistance. 683 000 people have been internally displaced because of the drought. as a result, humanitarian partners are now preparing for a possible influx of somali refugees to neighbouring countries. we must also be aware that the eu adheres to the principle that returns must be voluntary, dignified and sustainable. given the current context, that is a real challenge, a very huge challenge, and there may be further instability ahead for a country and a region already on the brink. we must collectively commend the host communities of dadaab, the people of kenya and their government for offering sanctuary to people fleeing violence, conflict and hunger. that is the message which i personally conveyed to the kenyan government and authorities when i visited dadaab last year. the government of kenya is a driver of regional initiatives and has shown willingness to find a collective solution to this issue, in line with international standards and principles. that point was made in the mogadishu declaration of 22 february 2017, jointly endorsed by the region’s presidents, and also at the igad summit, held in nairobi on 25 march this year, on sustainable solutions for somalian refugees. the eu has already welcomed the nairobi declaration. i would like to reiterate the importance of rapid implementation of the commitments underlying it. investment in development has to be increased and better coordinated, but that is not enough. policies need to be changed, especially for job access and for living outside the camps, as well as creating conditions in somalia allowing people to go home. i am glad to know that the spirit of the nairobi declaration is reflected in the resolution of this parliament. dear colleagues, another positive milestone was the london somalia conference on 11 may 2017, just two weeks ago. the agreement on a security pact and the new partnership for somalia was an important step forward. the european union has announced an additional eur 200 million for the period up to 2020. the eu trust fund is also providing eur 50 million in somalia to support the voluntary return of somalian refugees. of course, as the european union we remain engaged in providing humanitarian assistance in the dadaab camp and somalia, in parallel with development support to foster conditions conducive to return including security and access to basic services in somalia. the commission itself has supported humanitarian assistance to refugees in kenya with nearly eur 130 million since 1996 and eur 12.7 million this year alone. at the same time the eu has intensified programmes aimed at strengthening state building and stabilising somalia. in addition, in response to the security threats coming from terrorists in somalia, we are supporting various projects to counter violent extremists with an overall budget of eur 18 million. as i said, the eu acknowledges the generosity that kenya and other countries in the region have shown to somalian refugees. we hope that the kenyan government will continue to provide protection and asylum to refugees until they can voluntarily return home. we all need to collectively support the country doing this and to do so in a way that benefits both the refugees and the host communities in dadaab. we also need to make every effort to help consolidate peace in somalia. that is the only way to resolve the protracted refugee crisis in the region. i am grateful, as the commissioner for humanitarian aid, that parliament is continuing to support the common efforts to bring about a sustainable and lasting solution to the regional refugee crisis. i welcome the resolution tabled, which seeks to further support these measures. thank you so much for your attention to this statement. i am looking forward to our in-depth discussions that will help us to see together how to evaluate the situation in the dadaab camp.

the rapporteur. mr president, the french situation requires that we be available for comments, since we are in the process of forming a government with a high european density. i come to the report and i would like to welcome this agreement because it is a very important step between the three institutions and will allow the regulation to be applied in a concrete way at the beginning of 2018. this proposal was eagerly awaited by european citizens, who will now be able to travel with the services they subscribe to in their own country. the regulation will apply to services provided for remuneration; the principle of copyright is therefore sanctified and emphasised by this text, but we are introducing a new freedom which is very important, namely the freedom to move temporarily and to benefit temporarily from the services available in our place of residence, in our country of origin. the definition and means of verification of the member state of residence is a provision which is absolutely essential for the operation of this system. the text is sufficiently clear: service providers will have to verify the country of residence of subscribers and the checks will be carried out in accordance with european union rules, namely that they will not violate the rules on the protection of individual freedoms and data privacy. in this respect too, the text is very balanced. similarly, a system of verification waiver is also provided for in the case of an agreement between service providers and rightholders, provided that all rightholders of the content used by the service provider are effectively included in the agreement and that there is no fraud on the state of residence. in order to prevent abuse, the service provider will be able, if he wishes, to check in a closed list of possibilities, in particular by means of the ip address, whether there is no fraud in this agreement, in order to maintain the balance between the two aspects, copyright on the one hand, and freedom of movement for temporary travel on the other. i know the need for our digital single market to be able to reconcile the exercise of intellectual property rights with the free provision of commercial services. this regulation has thus succeeded in making a bet which many people find difficult for ideological reasons, but which, with a little common sense and the will not to impoverish european creation, can be applied without any difficulty. today i hope that we can all complete this text so that negotiations can begin between the three institutions, which will allow for rapid implementation. in this respect, i thank the commissioner for taking a step towards the various requests we had made in this regard and i hope that we will soon be able to implement this regulation, probably in 2018, as i said.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, portability allows a person subscribed to an online service to continue using it when he is temporarily away in another member state of the union. so the idea itself is interesting. however, there are a number of observations which should be noted with caution. firstly, the proposed text is a regulation and not a directive; it will therefore be particularly binding on the states. secondly, it may eventually call into question the right to geo-blocking which is a component of the sovereignty of states. in addition, it suffers from a serious internal contradiction in that it does not specify the maximum duration of stay in another state giving right to portability. the risk is that portability will become the norm rather than the exception. finally, the text risks encouraging global offers which will jeopardise the territoriality of copyright and reduce the diversity of offers. once again, the union will thus encourage the concentration of supply in favour of multinationals. for all these reasons, i shall vote against this text.

in writing. this text concerns a set of trade concessions for ukraine in the framework of the 'deep free trade area' which has been provisionally applied since 1 may 2016 as a result of the association agreement between the european union and ukraine. the report highlights the asymmetrical nature of the concessions made by the european union, which is reducing customs duties more rapidly than ukraine. the commission has also examined the impact of the measures on the union industry, in particular the impact of the measures on the union industry's sales and market share. these concessions consist of tariff-free quotas for certain agricultural products: wheat, barley, oats, natural honey, processed tomatoes, grape juice and maize. some industrial products are also partially exempted. these concessions threaten the economic equilibrium of certain sectors. in the case of maize in particular, this additional quota of 650 000 tonnes per year could cause prices to fall, since the european union is already in deficit with ukraine on its maize imports. it should be noted that the eu-ukraine association agreement is a symbol of a denial of democracy. the agreement was rejected by the dutch people in a referendum in april 2016, but was nevertheless adopted by the lower house of the dutch parliament on 30 may.

i'm the reporter. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am particularly pleased to present to you today my own-initiative report on the protection of vulnerable adults. in accordance with rule 46 of parliament's rules of procedure, it contains recommendations to the commission. this is a subject which has been of particular interest to me, as it deals with the problems and difficulties that european citizens may encounter or are encountering in the implementation of their rights. we must bear in mind that vulnerability may affect all of us, directly or indirectly, at some point. vulnerability can be physical or psychological. it may be the result of a life accident or be due to degenerative diseases related to old age. i strongly believe that, given the current difficulties facing the european union and its institutions, it is essential that the union should get closer to its citizens and deal with issues that directly concern them. protecting the most deprived among us seems to me a vital mission. in the committee on legal affairs, we agreed to define vulnerable adults as natural persons who have reached the age of 18 and are temporarily or permanently unable to manage their own person and/or property. this definition is the same as that of the hague convention of 13 january 2000. each eu member state has its own legal framework with different standards for the protection of vulnerable adults. however, the free movement of persons entails the creation of crossborder legal links, such as having a place of residence or assets abroad, working abroad, marrying a foreigner or marrying abroad, starting a family or divorcing in a member state other than the one of which one is a national, or simply retiring in another member state. the assets of vulnerable persons may be distributed across several member states, without there being a uniform legal framework within the union to protect their rights. the disparity of national laws too often delays decision-making concerning the privacy and personal life or health of vulnerable adults. this in fact creates obstacles to their freedom of movement and makes it impossible to protect their persons and property. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rights of the disabled are respected. the aim is not to harmonise existing protection measures in each member state, the establishment of which is a matter for the member states alone, but to put in place a set of legal rules to facilitate the information, recognition and enforcement of decisions concerning vulnerable adults in cross-border situations and to strengthen cooperation between member states in this field. the main objectives of this proposal for a recommendation are to promote the recognition of protection measures taken by the authorities of one member state in the other member states without the need to have recourse to an exequatur judgment. these are procedures that are time-consuming, costly and random; implement national files or registers listing administrative and judicial decisions on protection measures and, where they exist, ineligibility orders; to set up single union forms to promote information on administrative and judicial decisions concerning vulnerable adults; ensure that the sharing of information on the protection status of vulnerable adults between member states is carried out in compliance with the principle of confidentiality and the rules on the protection of personal data. in conclusion, i would remind you that at present, in international law, the legal instrument of reference for intra- and extra-community crossborder disputes concerning vulnerable adults is the hague convention of 13 january 2000. it entered into force on 1 january 2009. to date, some 15 states have signed it and only seven have ratified it in 8 years, namely germany, austria, estonia, the united kingdom, but only for scotland, finland, the czech republic and france. this is clearly insufficient to ensure its implementation. we hope that the commission will follow our recommendations. this would greatly facilitate the lives of vulnerable adults affected by cross-border situations. this would make life easier for those around them and for the professionals who are involved in these situations. thank you for them.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, the european population is ageing and vulnerable adults are therefore increasing in number. it is therefore a legitimate concern. the bergeron report is unfortunately not up to the task. the european parliament should have identified the legal solutions already implemented by some member states of the union and merely recommended that other states follow suit. this would have been a tribute to france, which has just ten years ago put in place an effective system of future protection mandates. the bergeron report was sacrificed to the federalist cult of uniformity. instead of respecting the freedom of each state, it deplores the fact that there are differences between national laws, without wanting to understand that this legal diversity is a cultural richness. the commission is proposing to draw up a regulation which will impose a standardised form of penalty, similar to the european form of the sickness and invalidity mandate which it is calling for. in the name of the principle of subsidiarity and, more profoundly, out of respect for national sovereignty, i shall therefore oppose this report.

the agenda calls for the joint debate on the digital economy with the report by nicola danti, on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, on the european agenda for the collaborative economy (2017/2003 (ini)) (a8-0195/2017) and the report by henna virkkunen and philippe juvin, on behalf of the committee on industry, research and energy, on online platforms and the digital single market (2016/2276 (ini)) (a8-0204/2017).
the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, colleagues, much has been said so far in this debate about platforms and the digital economy. i agree with all the points that have been made. the question of platforms is both simple and complicated. platforms are the key to the modern economy. they have considerable advantages for consumers, who can compare, who can buy and who have a freedom that they did not have before. they are an extraordinary opportunity for education and access to knowledge. we remember when we were students, when we didn't have these platforms and we had to spend hours in the library. all that is over. our entire society is evolving because of platforms. they are a positive and wonderful tool. at the same time, the question we are asking both the european parliament and the european commission is whether these platforms should be subject to a number of common rules in all eu countries. the first is the question of the homogenisation of european rules. it is clear that if we want a digital single market, we will need to have common rules and definitions in all eu countries. we have to talk about the same thing everywhere. if we do not make this effort to harmonise european law, including on definitions, we are either subject to a fragmentation of the law and therefore to a weakening of the platforms and the european economy, or we are subject to the good will of the judge who, through case law, will change the law, which we do not want. the second point, which is a key point, is the question of the responsibility of the platforms. you know that today, platforms are held accountable by rules that were enacted more than 15 years ago. the world has changed in 15 years. at that time, there were two types of host: active and inactive. clearly, this distinction no longer reflects reality. there are now many platforms that are not just storing data but are selecting it, recommending it, referencing it, monetizing it. our old rules are no longer appropriate, we need to change the rules of platform responsibility. the third point is the question of the protection of the users of these online platforms. it is essential to win the trust of these users, i.e. transparency, a level playing field and a high level of data protection. we remember the case of the blacklisting by a large web hosting company of a british company, which could no longer be seen on the market because this large web hosting company, which is a platform, had decided to promote its own company, which had the same economic activity. there must be transparency and the rules must be fair and shared. the fourth point concerns the question of the taxation of platforms. it is something fundamental. to move quickly on a complex subject, we want things to be simple and parliament will, i hope, support this proposal tomorrow by voting on our report. the platforms have to pay taxes in europe, where they have their customers or their users. then, of course, there is the question of vat. vat is a very smart old tax, except that it is totally unsuited to the digital economy, and especially the platform economy. we need to invent a new tax system that will give a boost to this new economy. finally, there is the question of b2b relations. it is clear that every effort must be made to prevent platforms that dominate very often concentrated markets from imposing unfair practices on new entrants. we want to avoid that. the market cannot regulate everything and we are waiting for the commission to make proposals. as you understand, ladies and gentlemen, the real question we are asking ourselves, together with henna virkkunen, is whether we want a digital single market, whether we want genuine european digital sovereignty, whether we want to see european champions emerge, whether we simply want to participate in the evolution of a new economy through new definitions and new rules for platforms.
on behalf of the enf group. madam president, the collaborative economy and the use of digital platforms are a real revolution for many economic sectors that are already highly destabilised. a balanced and non-partisan analysis should have taken stock of the opportunities offered by this new economic model, but above all should have paid particular attention to the immense risks it poses to millions of people. the concerns of the rapporteurs are facade-deep. the only thing they fear is the fragmentation of the single market, which they believe is threatened by uncoordinated legal responses by member states to try to regulate the sector. the collaborative economy is primarily the result of organised economic deregulation, a contraction in the real economy and wages, the explosion of unemployment and tax fraud. monetising private property is not a choice, but often becomes an economic necessity. the solutions proposed will therefore have no other use than political. they thus tend to guarantee only one thing: compliance with the european commission's timetable on the digital single market. the real issues at stake are forgotten: digital independence and network security, stability of the real economy and the labour market, protection of consumers and businesses, and the fight against fiscal dumping.
madam president, there is enormous potential in the collaborative economy, and europe has the potential to become a leader in this field. this new digital economy enables many retired people, young people, the unemployed, students and precarious employees to find employment and supplement their income. our entrepreneurs are inventing new services every day and we need to encourage the development of these start-ups. however, the question of the law applicable to such platforms needs to be clarified. the adjective 'collaborative' cannot be a marketing slogan which hides, in reality, a massive circumvention of social rules, unfair competition for our artisans and smes, deception of consumers and tax avoidance. a fair framework is therefore needed and we look forward to the concrete measures that the commission will propose in this regard.

been recognized for decades now. logic would have us come together to take into account the new economy, the economy of functionality, the economy of use, the economy that makes consumers - especially the poorest - no longer want to be forced to constantly change the products they buy and that break down as soon as the legal guarantees stop. so we have to take this new economy into account. we also in writing. this scandal shows that eu standards can be unenforceable despite praiseworthy intentions. the emis commission was set up in early 2016 with the volkswagen case and aimed to find out whether brussels or the member states were aware of the differences between european emission standards and the reality of emissions from engines of different european vehicle brands. the report of the committee of inquiry blames brussels and the member states for a lack of control over the practices of car manufacturers. however, most manufacturers would abuse the rule allowing them to reduce the efficiency of the pollution control systems in the event that they risk damaging the engine (article 5 of community regulation no 715/2007). the report also regrets that, while competition is free between national type-approval bodies, the eu does not have a supranational type-approval body. finally, the report of the commission of inquiry commended the compliance of american manufacturers with pollution standards comparable to european standards. the situation in the united states is not comparable, however, since the use of diesel is an ultra-minority among light vehicles. the nature of the strengthening of european standards in this area should therefore be kept in mind.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, colleagues, this report on the inspection system for ro-ro ferries and ferries is an opportunity to recall the terrible accident which took place at 1 a.m. on 28 september 1994 between tallinn and stockholm. on that day, in less than ten minutes, an uncontrolled opening of the cargo doors allowed water to enter the ferry estonia, which sank, killing 852 people. it's the deadliest passenger ship accident in europe after the titanic, and it happened less than 23 years ago. and this is not an isolated incident. a few years earlier, 193 people had died in a similar disaster off the port of zeebruges. and four years ago, 454 children died in a ferry sinking off the coast of south korea. in 2015, ports in the european union recorded 395 million maritime passengers. this is a considerable number, which is why it is essential that the safety of these passengers is ensured to the highest standards. this directive on a system of inspection for the safe operation of regular services of ro-ro ferries and high-speed passenger craft is an amendment to the port state control directive, which becomes the reference directive, and at the same time repeals the directive on a system of mandatory visits specific to ro-ro ferries. the first exercise was to simplify, rationalise and concentrate existing standards. we then strengthened and clarified the regulation, the key elements of the report being: clarification of responsibilities between the port state and the flag state avoiding duplication and legal loopholes; definition of the competent authority of the member state; clarification of the periodicity of inspections, which must take place twice a year, including one in operation, and every four to eight months. another new feature is that inspections of rolling stock and high-speed passenger craft are to be considered as a top priority in the annual inspection quota of the member states. an article on the consideration of risks to passengers and crew has been added to include an additional human element in these inspections. a commission wording allows delegated acts to be adopted, where necessary, under appropriate conditions. finally, we have an agreement on reinspections in the event of a change of ship's assignment. finally, a database will be set up to enable information to be exchanged as quickly as possible during ongoing inspections between member states. let me thank all the fictitious rapporteurs of the committee on transport and tourism for their work and excellent cooperation, the director-general of the european commission for his support and expertise, and of course the maltese presidency for its cooperation, its ambition to implement this triple directive and its ability to respond to the remarks and requests of the european parliament. in june last year, we quickly reached agreement on this directive in a trilogue. i hope that it will receive a massive vote in our parliament.

, rapporteur for the opinion of the juri committee. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate my colleague, mrs daniela aiuto, for presenting in her report the objectives we set ourselves in the legal affairs committee, namely the maintenance of a high level of safety on board ships and the preservation of passenger confidence. as part of the simplification process carried out by the commission, many of the definitions contained in the directive have been adapted to current circumstances, in particular because of technological developments in the field of maritime transport. this is particularly true of shipbuilding materials. in its original version, the directive applied, for example, only to ships made of steel and equivalent materials, but it was not implemented in the same way in all member states, in breach of the safety rules. the proposal therefore clarifies the scope of the directive as regards the definition of aluminium as an equivalent and stronger material other than steel, in order to achieve high and common safety standards for all these vessels. the aim is therefore to raise the level of safety for passenger ships, and this european initiative should be welcomed.

circular economy model by converting waste into nutrients, thus reducing the european union's dependence on nutrients imported from third countries. the aim of this proposal is to establish conditions of competition for organic fertilisers on a par with those for mineral fertilisers. the second objective is to establish limit levels of contaminants in fertilisers. the rates proposed by the commission are unrealistic and dangerous for the industry which uses phosphate as a natural source for the preparation of its secondary fertilisers. the french organic or secondary fertiliser industry is highly developed and has every interest in benefiting from the opening of the internal market and the award of the ce mark. these economic operators are de facto subject to a distortion of competition in the market for mineral and chemical fertilisers. the support obtained by french civil society on this issue is a sign of the real stakes for this particular sector of the french economy, and i would like to thank them here. on the other hand, the support of french members of parliament from all political parties in this house is still expected from the players in this sector. in addition to the vital stakes for the french phosphate fertiliser industry, the commission's proposal would also be a bad idea to make us dependent on only one source of phosphate supply and the collapse of the north african phosphate market could have serious repercussions on the social balance of these countries. the geopolitical interest is also an important issue in this text. our group has tabled amendments to set the cadmium level at 80 milligrams per kilogram, with a gradual reduction over 15 years to 60 milligrams, a reasonable and pragmatic timeframe for research and development, particularly in phosphate decadmiation techniques. the french delegation of the national front will not be able to choose tomorrow, when voting, to sacrifice too many french jobs by an ideological logic lacking common sense, by choosing cadmium levels that are far too low. it is probably better for the french secondary and organic fertiliser industry to accept the status quo by remaining temporarily excluded from the single market, rather than risking many of its employees being made redundant. the exploitation of an economic need for the benefit of conflicting objectives does not seem to me to be the best way of helping the european industrial fabric.

whistleblowers, considering that we should not be attached to a particular situation employees, subcontractors, consultants , but rather to the nature of the information that is revealed, and therefore consider that from the moment a whistleblower discloses information about actions contrary to the general european interest, at that moment, he must be protected. what protection for whistleblowers? we know that very often when we speak, we are under enormous pressure, even retaliation. it is therefore necessary to make clear that such retaliation is punishable by criminal law and to ensure that it is punished and that the harm caused to whistleblowers and those around them is fully compensated. we also want whistleblowers to be able to receive financial legal support when needed. we see that in many cases they have to face extremely degraded living conditions, loss of jobs, sale of houses, reduced resources. that is why we must also be able to provide financial support in certain cases, but also psychological help, because it is always a challenge to deal with organisations which have enormous resources - enormous means of action and means of pressure. we also want to take this need to rebalance the balance of power into account when an employee whistleblower is subject to measures within his company, so that it is up to the employer to provide guarantees that this is not a matter of retaliation. we make an important proposal: we want to set up independent authorities to welcome, help and advise whistleblowers. as we said, they are often in a fragile situation and left to themselves in the face of powerful organisations and, therefore, this network of independent authorities, with an independent european authority that could provide coordination and a way of appeal for whistleblowers, seems to us particularly important. i would like to take as an example a case which we shall also be discussing this week, but which is of a different nature. i think about all those people who have been exposed to the damage caused by glyphosate. i am thinking in particular of mrs grataloup, who tried to alert the monsanto company to the wrongdoing, who this report any possibility of using the press. it is clear that it is precisely in the most problematic cases, in the most serious cases, in the most serious cases - we are talking about corruption, we are talking about embezzlement - that it is necessary to alert the press; these are the cases where the whistleblowers are most exposed. what sense would it make to want to remove the protection of
