reduction has stagnated. in some countries the numbers are even on the rise, and this is unacceptable. we do have to find a new way forward. enforcement of rules by member states on speeding, drink driving, safety belts and other unsafe driver behaviour has already had a positive effect. this is also the case for improving driver training and road infrastructure. the report rightly concludes that these are areas for improvement. the commission fully agrees with those conclusions, and this is why we have recently proposed new measures, for example on the training of professional drivers. but there is more good news. commission services have been preparing a revision of the general safety regulation and a pedestrian safety regulation. this has been done in a totally transparent and open manner by involving all relevant stakeholders from day one. in essence, we performed the ultimate peer reviewing exercise before deciding on what we should do and how. we have received very broad support from the european parliament in this report, but also from the member states’ road safety advocacy groups, and last but not least, the automotive industry itself. let us focus now on the accident avoidance technologies. advanced technologies can help us a lot in preventing traffic accidents from happening all together. one of the most effective technologies available today is automatic or autonomous emergency braking. the car stops completely by itself when it sees that an accident is about to happen. this way, a collision between two cars can be prevented. another technology that we are looking at is emergency lane-keeping system. it detects that that car has drifted out of its lane for whatever reason, on a collision course, and steers the car back into its own lane. in fact, these two advanced systems will also be used for automated and connected driving. speeding is one the main killers on our roads. this is why we are also looking into a ground breaking technology such as intelligent speed assistance. another major challenge for road safety is how to effectively deal with drivers who are too distracted to drive safely by themselves. this was not explicitly developed in the report, but it deserves our attention too. we know about the increase in road fatalities due to growing use of smart phones while driving. therefore, driver distraction and fatigue monitoring systems are also firmly on our radar. the eu will absolutely be at the forefront of car safety when these safety measures are out into effect. these measures already have a huge potential to protect eu citizens, as standard equipment on all passenger cars. but we should not stop there. the second item i would like to discuss with you is the protection of pedestrians and cyclists in traffic. we must have seen and heard terrible stories of trucks running over children at road crossings and hitting cyclists when making a turn. it is time that we recognise the urgent need for a comprehensive approach to protect the most vulnerable road users against current truck designs, such as blind spots. a first step is to add special detection systems to heavy duty vehicles that will know when pedestrians and cyclists are in the vehicle’s blind spot zone. but the second step is the most important one: designing larger windows. our analyses show that when a driver can see the danger directly, accidents with pedestrians and cyclists are prevented. with these two steps together, we are looking at a revolutionary approach to make trucks in cities a lot safer for pedestrians and cyclists. the work to draft the new proposed vehicle safety legislation is now in progress, and we aim at including it in the third mobility package coming next year. all in all, the commission is taking all measures which are in our competent to address this silent killer on eu roads. it is our responsibility to do more. we expect that other actors will play their part as well – especially member state authorities – when it comes to education, training, enforcement and infrastructure safety. so once again, let me thank the honourable member for such an excellent report that supports this important work, and i do hope that i can count on your continued support and engagement in the coming months.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would first like to thank mr dieter-lebrecht koch for his excellent report and, of course, to recall the important issue of road safety. i would like to return to two specific points, which i think are important, without going back to the many human and technical factors which could be solutions and which the commissioner has described in detail. first, the recognition of the intrinsic dependence between accidents and the quality of infrastructure, in particular the quality of the road network. for example, motorways, despite their high speed and high vehicle concentration, account for only 5% of serious accidents, demonstrating the direct relationship between road safety and nature and the quality of infrastructure. as a reminder, a recent study looked at the financial situation of the road haulage industry in europe. 270 billion in revenue for the states per year, 160 billion in investment, including maintenance, from all taxes combined. so it is the missing 110 billion that could be useful to improve the missing infrastructure. it should also be noted that road accidents, while breaking up families, also represent a high cost to society, especially in terms of health expenditure. where the emphasis is often on the enforcement resources available to the states, which are also a source of additional revenue in the billions to improve road safety, public authorities should also do their job better upstream, investing more in risk prevention and saving lives. my second point concerns the lack of awareness among the medical profession. i speak here as a former doctor. everyone knows, of course, that alcohol and drugs are dangerous when driving, but it seems to either to disabilities which have not been taken into account or to treatments whose consequences on the ability to drive have not been highlighted. this is another point worth considering.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased that we are discussing relations between the european union and africa today, ahead of the eu/au summit in abidjan, côte d'ivoire, on 29 and 30 november. it will be an important summit and it is crucial that the european parliament's voice can be heard in this context. i should like to begin by thanking my fictitious colleagues for their cooperation. we have reached a balanced text which presents a strong position of the european parliament on the need to renew our partnership with africa. one of the major recommendations in our report is the need to strengthen political dialogue with the african continent. i am convinced that political dialogue must be increased between the two continents in order to establish a win-win partnership that responds to common challenges in a spirit of mutual sharing and respect. a paradigm shift is needed to move beyond the donor-recipient approach to an equal partnership approach. in this relationship between the european union and africa, we must nevertheless recognise the special links between us and the acp group of states. this is why we recall in our report the need to maintain this acquis, while improving it and strengthening the regional dimension in the post-cotonou process. while political dialogue needs to be strengthened to have a relationship that responds to shared challenges, this also requires making resilience a central focus of cooperation between the two continents. this resilience must be addressed in the five dimensions: political, security, economic, environmental and social. to promote political resilience, governance and respect for human rights should be the cornerstones of our partnership with africa and more frequent political exchanges between the different mixed parliamentary assemblies should be supported, so that there is no taboo. the security issue is also crucial in our relationship with africa. as we point out in the report, there are close links between development and security. without security there can be no development and vice versa. it is therefore necessary to strengthen cooperation between the two continents to combat organised crime, trafficking in human beings and terrorism. while the european union is a major player in ensuring security on the african continent, all african countries and regional organisations must also be involved in peace and security. it is important that africa builds its own capacities. a major challenge is also to ensure the economic resilience of both continents by creating quality jobs. this must be achieved through investments in key sectors such as the blue economy, research, digitalisation, but also energy, basic infrastructure and agriculture. the decisive role of the private sector and smes is emphasized in our report, because we all know that it is necessary to create wealth on the african continent. and this wealth created must remain there. every year, more than $50 billion is illegally smuggled out of africa. this is more than official development assistance. we need to strengthen the tools to fight tax evasion and corruption, which are a prerequisite for sustainable development. environmental and social resilience are also important elements of our report. in addition to the demographic challenges we need to address, the issue of climate change is crucial for the african continent, given the increasing number of natural disasters in the last 10 years and their increased intensity. finally, migration and mobility are issues in our relationship with africa which we cannot avoid. the migration flows we know must be better controlled and not suffered. i believe it is important that the phenomena be tackled in a coordinated and comprehensive way between the two continents, involving the countries of origin, transit and destination, in order to make it a tool for the development of the two continents, which requires a long-term approach. finally, several european initiatives are worth mentioning, such as the edf, the various trust funds and migration partnerships, which should help to combat the root causes of irregular migration. in order to put in place sustainable solutions, it is urgent that the member states participate financially in the various funds set up at european level, as president juncker has recalled. there are many challenges to overcome if the 218 million people living in extreme poverty on the african continent are to be lifted out of it. this is a challenge we must face together and i sincerely hope that the next summit in abidjan will provide answers.

2018 budget in the early hours of the morning on the night of 17-18 november. once again we have been able to measure the narrowness of our room for manoeuvre in a particularly tight budgetary framework, but, ladies and gentlemen, we have reasons for satisfaction which i would like to share with you. first of all, the mid-term review is not a bible. each year's budget discussion gives us the opportunity to get back to work. in other words, the european parliament retains its prerogatives to discuss the budget each year. secondly, we have managed to erase the cuts made by the council, by reinstating the majority of the appropriations it had cut in order to preserve margins for alleged unforeseen expenditure, in particular the extension of the budgetary facility for turkey to allow that country to host syrian refugees. we reached an agreement because our priority was to re-fund the programmes under heading 1a, those that are the best performing, those that prepare our future and protect europeans: research through horizon 2020, youth mobility through erasmus, erasmus+ and erasmus pro - two programmes which, unfortunately, are frustrating because we do not have the means to on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, we will adopt, by an accelerated procedure, the conditions for the introduction of ifrs 9, which is an accounting standard for the transfer of incurred losses to expected losses, which has a direct impact on the accounting of loan losses. mr karas has just recalled that parliament, in its resolution of 6 december 2016, had requested such a procedure to adapt the conditions for the introduction of ifrs 9 in the financial statements, since this accounting standard will enter into force on 1 january next year. it was important to recognise that the transitional arrangements were necessary, because a sudden increase in provisions for expected credit losses would have led to a sharp weakening of regulatory capital ratios, at the very time when we are asking banks to consolidate them. but we need to look beyond this, because while this regulation mitigates the negative impact on banks' regulatory capital, the question of the impact of this standard on the financial stability of the union remains, even though the iasb has not yet carried out impact assessments. we will therefore have to take up a number of concerns which are already on the table as regards the risks of procyclical effects of this standard when a recession period begins, or as regards the question of the alteration of the distribution of credits between activities, or the risk of shortening the maturity of loans. this leads us, as parliament, in the same way as we said when ifrs 9 was adopted, to reiterate our call for a serious assessment of the impact of this standard, beyond the amendment which will already, as we know, be proposed next year. we must ensure that this standard does not weaken the conditions for longterm investment. this is perhaps why we want to ask the commission to look at the impact assessment of this standard without delay. in this context, we should recall the recommendations of the maystadt report, which called for us to reject on behalf of the enf group. mr president, the ifrs 9 accounting standard will significantly increase the volatility of bank balance sheets, particularly those of french banks. ifrs 9 will have a significant procyclical effect by generalising fair value instead of historical value. rules such as ifrs 9 are part of a multifaceted arsenal designed to weaken banking intermediation in financing the economy and to encourage its replacement by financing markets under the control of us actors. moreover, this rule will increase the propensity of large banks to approach a default when political timelines in a given country would make it possible to foresee that eurosceptic parties, which would of course not please the financial markets, would be on their way to being elected. we want strong banks, but ifrs 9 does not allow that. this rule, on the contrary, makes banks more vulnerable. we cannot continue any longer the process of weakening and dismantling the banks of continental europe, and especially french banks, for the greater benefit of american banks. in these circumstances, the simon report, which de facto amounts to a five-year delay in the application of ifrs 9, is therefore very positive and that is why we will support it.
the rapporteur. mr president, i will not, in the introduction to this debate, go over all the steps which led to our adoption, i hope, tomorrow of this amendment to the instrument for stability and peace. i will simply remind you that this is a process that started almost four years ago now, since it was at the council in december 2013 that the high representative considered an instrument to finance equipment for armed forces with which we have european union missions working on security and development. i would like to begin by thanking all the coordinators and members who have been involved in the work on this text. i would also like to thank our chairman of the committee on foreign affairs, mr mcallister, who led the trilogue negotiations, negotiations which were swift and fruitful. the commission has made a very considerable effort to find funding to meet parliament's requests, and i would like to thank all the parties involved in this very fruitful trilogue. to return to the substance of this instrument, i would point out that it is the missing link in the chain of european union instruments in the field of security and development. we now have missions with the armed forces in certain developing countries, missions which provide training but are not able to do so, which do not have the legal, practical or financial tools to provide equipment - which i would point out is not lethal - civilian equipment which enables these armed forces to support development operations, because we are talking about countries in which no development is possible without the assistance of the armed forces: mali, somalia, niger, the central african republic and many others unfortunately. i would also like to point out that the discussions we had were extremely rich and interesting, and that many points of view were expressed. i had a more ambitious vision for this instrument, and that's no secret. we have reached a compromise, which i think is a good compromise, and i would like to thank the groups who have participated. i also wanted to remind you because i always hear arguments that you should not be bad faith. firstly, this instrument is very well regulated legally, financially and politically. we can't do whatever we want and whatever with this instrument. secondly, this instrument is not used to finance the purchase or supply of arms. this is equipment that is non-lethal. i still see and read in the press, in particular, arguments which are totally biased, which are totally incorrect. the european union is not going to finance the purchase of arms in developing countries, that is not what this is about. we're talking about nonlethal equipment here. i say this very solemnly, very firmly, because i would not want to leave any doubt in this regard, and i would not have allowed the adoption of a text which would go in this direction. so we have a text which is balanced, which is strictly controlled, which is modest - it must be remembered that this is a substantial contribution in principle, but modest in financial terms, we are talking about 100 million for three years. and we also have a contribution today which does not exhaust the debate to come, and i say this in particular to the groups which had reservations: yes, we will need a more sustainable system in the future and this can be the subject of a political debate in the coming periods. but for now, i think we can be satisfied with the tool we have put in place, which will be very useful in practice for the european union missions deployed in these sensitive countries.
mr president, this proposal has the merit of seeking to strengthen the link between security and development that the european security strategy established in 2003. the security of a country is a necessary condition for its development. as charles péguy said, "order, and order alone, is freedom". the proposal is clearly intended to enable the european union to support the military forces of developing countries. at a time when islamist terrorism is destabilising many countries, particularly in africa, this initiative may at first seem relevant, but we must be clear-minded and know what we want. this proposal is part of a strategy to extend the eu's influence over the foreign and defence policies of its member states. i believe that foreign affairs and national defence must remain a matter for the sovereignty of states. this is a matter of principle, particularly for france, which remains a major diplomatic and military power. but it is also wise, because the union lacks realism. it has already failed to stop immigration from libya, to the point that italy had to take its place to solve the problem through a bilateral agreement. it is also giving moral lessons to the whole world and we shall soon see that its moralism will cause the failure of its policy of intervention. history teaches us that empires always end badly.
the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, i thank all the colleagues who have taken part in this debate, of course, but also those who have contributed to the preparation of this text to enrich it and to make it a compromise, which i believe is entirely virtuous and useful. to those who are opposed to this text, i would like to say that i obviously respect all opinions and oppositions, but they must be in good faith and really be based on what is in the text and on the reality we are working on. there is no mention in the text that we are going to finance military equipment. we're going to finance civilian equipment for military forces. the reality is that we're going to fund hospitals and we're going to fund communications systems. is this military hardware? of course not! is it also useful to civilian populations? of course you can! that's what we're talking about. i would like the many colleagues who spoke against the text to read it first, to see what is in it and what is not, and to know a little about the reality of the countries in question. in mali, when you have a mission of the european union that trains malian soldiers, but cannot provide them with equipment - the malian army loses a soldier a day or a week - to treat these soldiers, do you think that this is contributing to the militarization of development? frankly, it's not honest to say that. it is not fair and it is not right in relation to the reality we are talking about. i hear colleagues say: 'we are going to militarize development aid through this instrument'. what are we talking about? it should be remembered that the development aid, the edf, is 31 billion euros. the instrument in question is eur 100 million. who can speak of the militarization of development with this instrument which does not even allow for the purchase of lethal equipment and weapons? once again, i think we have reached a very strict compromise, very legally framed and very politically binding. i thank all the colleagues who took part in it and i would like those who continue to oppose it for ideological reasons to show a little more pragmatism and realism to really see the needs we are meeting with this instrument.
mr president, a few days ago i was visiting the port of sète. it is the flower of the occitanie region's economy, generating over 2 000 jobs and seeing its activity increase by 17% over the last three years. it offers its territory a window on the world and valuable dynamism for the regional economy, both industrially and in terms of fishing or tourism. however, the free trade agreements imposed by the european union are now paying a heavy price: the brutal and unannounced competition of a local industry against foreign productions. here, the reduction in customs duties for argentine biofuel has a direct effect of a drop in activity of more than 30%. a hundred employees are on the hook and the life pool is now directly affected. i therefore call on the commission to commit itself to preserving local employment, to change course and finally to defend the interests of citizens and local industrial tools by genuinely protecting our internal markets at european level and by solidarity. solidarity is the opposite of competition.
mr president, the banking union is designed to cut off the possibility of mutual support between commercial banks and their home member state. this deepening of federalism comes after the breakdown of the political and economic link between european nations and their central banks, which dates back to the maastricht treaty, and prohibits any possibility of direct support of a state by its central bank. in both cases, the aim is to eliminate any financial recourse and economic support that a state might receive, in order to increase the pressure on the financial markets. market discipline must, in the german spirit, oblige the states to adopt fiscal austerity policies. conversely, since the brrd, it has been permanently forbidden for states to support their banks in the event of financial difficulties. we believe it is crucial to go backwards. the european union will never succeed in creating a functioning banking union. it is therefore in the interest of citizens and states to dismantle the banking union as soon as possible. rearranging the internal legal order of the states in order to harmonise the hierarchy of bank creditors is therefore not going in the right direction. we believe that voting against this text is a vote of consistency in defending savers against the leasing system.
mr president, when this parliament adopted the directive on bank recovery and resolution in the event of bankruptcy, our concern was to avoid contagion and access to taxpayers' money by allowing for internal bailouts. at the same time, to make this viable, market conditions have been worsened or, in some ways, strengthened with the rise of both european legislation and international standards, with the prospect of the entry into force of the ftaa. we therefore had to organise the build-up of a market that would allow the players to be ready to have the debt quality to meet these obligations. in fact, several member states had launched their own reform in anticipation of the european response, and the banking sector, since the agreement at the financial stability board (fsb) at the end of 2015, was affected by the tlac requirement. the markets themselves - as evidenced by the large volumes of tlac-eligible debt successfully issued by banks - reacted and anticipated the effects of this reform. the idea is to allow banks to build up subordinated debt cushions that improve their solvency without unduly constraining their cost of funding. that is why i think we can be glad that this parliament has helped to implement this new type of debt in an accelerated way so that the players can prepare. of course, there have been issues raised in trying to use this accelerated vehicle which we will have to deal with when we tackle the substantive revision of the brrd directive but, at this stage, i believe that the key is to allow market players and the market itself to anticipate the entry into force of the new international standards.
mr president, we have indeed experienced repeated banking crises, which were also remedied by the taxpayers, and it seems to me that it is high time for europe to legislate first to protect consumers and their deposits, then to enable banks to guarantee their internal stability, but it seems to me even more important, on the other hand, to enable banks to lend to the economic world in order to revive employment in europe. the legislative text has the merit of being balanced to meet these three objectives. by implementing a hierarchy of creditors we will stabilise the banking system, but we must not forget that we need a regulatory central bank in europe and parliamentary control of all banking movements.
mr president, a civilization can be judged by the way it treats the most vulnerable, particularly the disabled, and europe still has a lot of progress to make in this area. i thank mrs stevens for inspiring this beautiful report on the european strategy for the millions of disabled people living in the european union. i agree with most of its proposals, which are almost always respectful of the sovereignty of states. in particular, i agree with the request to them to ensure accessibility for persons with disabilities to public buildings, public services and communication technologies, in accordance with the requirements of the un convention of 13 december 2006. i myself have seen to it that it is applied on the ground, as a councillor. i do, however, regret that this report is sometimes polluted by considerations which have nothing to do with it, such as paragraph 22 which refers - and i quote - to the multiple discrimination arising from the intersection of gender, disability and sexual orientation. i think the lgbti lobby could have had the grace to hide from the real subject of the report: disability.
mr president, disability is too serious a subject to be satisfied with long and repetitive statements of intent. i therefore fully support the desire to implement the principles of the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities as soon as possible. in addition, national regulations and laws already exist. it is therefore in each state that it is necessary to ensure their effective application. as such, the european commission will hardly be credible in calling for, for example, stricter legal obligations on accessibility to public buildings, given the budgetary austerity that brussels imposes on a number of member states. although this report is quite comprehensive, it is regrettable that no mention is made of the mobility of disabled people on a daily basis. the importance of financial aid for the adaptation of vehicles, or the promotion of carpooling in companies between able-bodied and disabled people, could have been mentioned.
in writing. the aim of this text is to achieve a total absence of discrimination for disabled people in the context of a barrier-free europe, with actions in two stages: 2017-2020 and 2020-2030. i am of course in principle in favour of such a move. but make no mistake, this text has a very different scope: the creation of a market involving 120 million people, worth over €30 billion! i personally, as a disabled person with a visual impairment, would like to see this subject not exploited. i also regret the semantic difficulties encountered in the text on the definition of disability. disability is the sum of functional and/or cognitive deficits and not, as the text claims, the sum of the obstacles which society must remove in order for the disabled person to have a normal life. i therefore regret that this text has led to a normative cacophony and, more broadly, that it exploits the problem of disability and disabled people to justify captive markets.

in writing. it would appear that the ins and outs of the european social pillar of social rights (espr) are not evolving despite the work done in the committee on employment and social affairs (empl). the epsr always seems to reflect the need for the european union to make a paradigm shift towards a strong european social model: clearly, harmonisation and therefore unfortunately a leveling down! europe has existed for many years, and each of its member states (not member states but sovereign states) has successfully adapted its social model to its own needs, taking into account the specific characteristics of each profession. we must preserve these particularities and aim upwards by exchanging good practices, not by deconstructing them! beyond harmonisation, i denounce a more serious underlying desire: that of propaganda aimed at making the eu look like the only solution to the problems of citizens, the desire to save a damaged european project, without carrying out the necessary reforms in depth.
on behalf of the efdd group. mr president, commissioner, the commission declared a year ago that the sustainable development goals (sdgs) were integrated into all its 10 priorities. yet the eurostat report shows that in just five years, five sdgs have shown significant progress, such as sdg 7 'clean and affordable energy', sdg 12 'responsible consumption and production' and sdg 3 'good health and well-being'. the remaining eight objectives are not making significant progress. these include sdg 4 'quality education', sdg 1 'no poverty', sdg 2 'zero hunger' and sdg 5 'gender equality'. worse, we learn that due to insufficient data, four sdgs cannot even be studied. let us be clear: states remain best placed to achieve the objectives they have approved themselves.
mr president, mr minister, mr commissioner, natural disasters and risks know no borders. we have too often been in reaction and not in anticipation. european solidarity in the face of disasters must be expressed in strong actions. this is what is being committed today, at your instigation, commissioner, and i congratulate you on this, with the €280 million committed until 2020 and the implementation of an autonomous capacity reserve. i was going to say 'finally' because i am one of those who have been calling for several years now for the pooling of capacities and the strengthening of resources for a stronger european civil protection. i am thinking here of a european fleet of canadair, a project which i also support with great enthusiasm, together with my colleague renaud muselier, president of the provence-alpes-côte d'azur region. water bombers in the colours of europe would be a strong symbol of a concrete europe, to the aid of the people. i am also thinking of the european network of civil protection and risk management hubs, which is the result of the preparatory action i presented to the european parliament and which was approved in the 2018 budget of the european union. the commissioner, the french air base at nîmes-garons, which you know well because you inaugurated it, a jewel of french civil security, could serve here as the first pilot base at european level to accommodate new capabilities. it is now up to the member states - as has already been said - to say concretely how they intend to contribute to the efforts we are making. that is why i have asked the president of the french republic to speak on this subject, so that france can make a concrete case at european level for the need to prevent risks better and, above all, to protect with reactivity through renewed means.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am divided tonight: i am both happy and sad. i am naturally delighted with the result of our work. we will adopt a strong and comprehensive report tomorrow on the fight against sexual abuse and sexual exploitation of children, an area where we absolutely need to move forward and redouble our efforts. i would naturally like to thank, from the bottom of my heart, our rapporteur, with whom we are fighting these issues on a daily basis, particularly in the intergroup on the rights of the child. i would like to thank her for her work and her strong commitment in all these areas. but at the same time i am saddened tonight because the reason we are having this debate is that the situation is far from satisfactory. since 2011, we have a directive that is a real step forward, but we are almost in 2018 and the results are disappointing: late transposition, incomplete transposition by the states, member states that have still not modernised their criminal law in relation to all these new forms of offences in the field of sexual exploitation of children, little done in terms of prevention and assistance to victims and a still too slow withdrawal of sexual abuse content. we are told that the directive has not reached its full potential, but how can we be satisfied with such a response? government and ngo reports are overwhelming, the numbers of exploitation are alarming, the victims are younger and younger, the content is increasing, so there is a need to redouble our efforts against these atrocities. i would like to emphasize three points. first, prevention: how can we prevent abuse, which often occurs in the immediate family environment? how can such rapes be prevented? how can we best protect our children before they fall prey to these criminal networks and predators? secondly, with regard to content on the internet, member states must ensure that child abuse content is promptly removed at source and they must have functional removal notification procedures. thirdly, training of actors: judicial and police actors must be sufficiently equipped by the member states to adapt to the evolving and terrible nature of these crimes. in conclusion, child actors must also be supported in order to detect victims, because this is absolutely dramatic for the construction of these children, who risk remaining and are too often invisible victims.
in writing. the figures for paedophilia are alarming, with over 13 percent of girls and 5.7 percent of boys reportedly being abused. and the situation is only going to get worse as europe faces a record influx of isolated miners to its coasts, the latter being, of course, the prime targets of traffickers. the most firm action is required against the perpetrators of such acts. however, not only has the european union not carried out a comprehensive evaluation of the effectiveness of the 2011 directive, but many additional measures would be needed to effectively combat these abuses. thus, while australia has recently introduced exit bans on persons convicted of paedophilia, it is inconceivable that european states do not also crack down on sex tourism, which, in addition to the human tragedies it causes, permanently tarnishes the image of western states in the regions affected by these practices. at a time when france is questioning the age of consent, it is also urgent to address the root cause by opposing the hypersexualization of children and, in particular, young girls, which is a worrying deviation from demanding feminism.
mr president, i would first like to thank the rapporteur, mrs notis marias, and our fictitious rapporteur, mrs jude kirton-darling, who has focused all our contributions on this report on the activities of the committee on petitions. this committee, on which i would like to dwell briefly, although it is not a legislative body, is essential for our institution because it ensures a fundamental right, guaranteed by our founding treaty, which is to petition when the right which we, the legislators, vote on here is not respected or calls for adjustments. this right is an essential link with our fellow citizens and civil society and requires the mobilisation of all actors to ensure that petitions are dealt with properly and diligently. we reviewed the working methods of the committee on petitions in 2015 to this end and they are working well. i therefore think we must reject amendments which would restrict our work and limit this democratic right to petition. if all the institutions must be mobilised - this parliament, the first - there is one which must adhere to a particular requirement, namely the european commission, because as guardian of the treaties it has the power to open infringement proceedings and to pursue member states before the court of justice for failure to act, if necessary. this power is also a responsibility towards our fellow citizens, not all of whom have the means to go to court. it is therefore also a responsibility towards this parliament, as a co-legislator, to ensure that european law is properly applied and to ensure the proper functioning of european democracy. for these reasons, we ask the european commission to ensure that it too deals diligently with the petitions we address to it and that it is as firm as possible in initiating infringement proceedings. it is a question of the proper functioning of european democracy and of respect for the texts we are voting on here as legislators.
for the greens/efa group mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, remember that not so long ago, in 2009-2010, europe was the leader in the fight against global warming; we were voting for a climate-energy package to set a course for our industry in terms of energy efficiency. but what have we done since then? the numbers don't lie, though. from 1990 to 2015, transport emissions increased by 16%. since 2015, it is the only sector that is still growing. transport accounts for 25% of europe's greenhouse gas emissions, 70% of which is road transport. air pollution causes 400 000 premature deaths in europe every year. it costs healthcare between €330 and €940 billion a year. but we have to do something to change that. it's now! i would remind you that in 2011 your commission committed itself to reducing co2 emissions from transport by 60% by 2050 compared to 1990. but how? this is where we must be firm and we have a good roadmap with mr eickhout's report. we should stop funding diesel research, even the head of volkswagen is now saying so. the same applies to aviation: let us tax kerosene at last, let us stop this vat discount on tickets. instead, let us put in place the 'polluter pays' principle, particularly in road transport, by charging on the basis of distance rather than time. let us set mandatory quotas for the production of clean vehicles for car manufacturers rather than encouraging them to do so. unfortunately, when reading your commission's proposals on co2 emissions from vehicles, it seems that europe is waiting for the market to do wonders, while china has decided to produce a minimum of 10% of electric vehicles by 2019. it is fine to criticise mr donald trump for his climate commitments, but it is better for europe to take the lead on climate change and set an example. i therefore ask you, ladies and gentlemen, to follow our rapporteur, mr eickhout, in reaffirming our firm ambition. our objective must be clear: to actually reduce co2 emissions from transport in europe. commissioner, i say this with great firmness: we cannot dance on a volcano any longer, it is now or never.
mr president, i thank the rapporteur for his work. i agree with a number of its proposals, such as the requirement for clear transport price signals, in application of the 'polluter pays' and 'user pays' principles. however, this seems to me to be difficult to reconcile with the progressive liberalisation of the various transport sectors within the european union. it is also paradoxical to want to reduce emissions while the european union is promoting, through the trans-european transport network programme, the acceleration of the integration of the new member states and the achievement of an internal market, ideally without barriers. finally, i regret that no mention is made of the question of the mobility of workers, which is being unreasonably encouraged by the european union. this worrying phenomenon results in an increasing demand for mobility and therefore for additional co2 emissions, whereas jobs should be protected in each country, but this would still require the will to do so.
mr president, the european union is the most advanced region in the world in terms of environmental standards and the fight against climate change. this does not mean that it should rest on its laurels. on the contrary, it requires it to go further and further to lead the way and, above all, to ensure that all its member states respect and apply the legislation. in this respect, the european strategy for low-emission mobility must be ambitious and comprehensive. the report on which we are voting in a few hours is demanding and realistic. it proposes concrete action. it is a document on which legislators can rely when declining our intentions in binding texts. his field is too wide to go into detail in a half-hour. i shall therefore concentrate on one aspect which i consider essential: the application of the 'polluter pays' and 'user pays' principles. transport generates pollution, that is a fact, and even if we can try to reduce it, it will never be zero. transport will always require ad hoc infrastructure, especially as vehicles become more sophisticated. however, we can try to reduce pollution at source, but to do this effectively, we need a binding minimum target for manufacturers, otherwise it will remain a wishful thinking. this will also benefit the competitiveness of the european automotive industry, as it will remain at the forefront of technological innovation. in addition, it is essential to have the infrastructure and the negative effects, known as 'external costs', financed by those who use it. if not, the taxpayers are paying the price, and that is deeply unfair. these principles are also enshrined in the treaty. i therefore support their implementation for all vehicles in europe.

member of the commission. – madam president, the european union has repeatedly expressed to the vietnamese authorities, including at the highest levels, its concerns over limitations to freedom of expression, both online and offline, as reflected in frequent cases of intimidation and violence against journalists and civil society activists. the eu has been constructively engaged with the vietnamese authorities on a revision of the penal code and its related laws, in order to ensure alignment with international standards by providing input to the national assembly, by offering exchange of best practices, and by promoting joint actions with like-minded countries. political and civil rights, as well as legal and judicial reform, are regularly raised at the human rights dialogue with vietnam. during the last session, which took place on 1 december 2017 in hanoi, the eu reiterated its request for all vietnamese citizens detained for peacefully exercising their freedom of expression to be released. in this context, the eu also referred to a number of individual cases. furthermore, the eu stressed that the negative trend in freedom of expression needs to be reversed, especially at a time when vietnam and the eu are committed to working towards a closer relationship. the case of mr nguyen van hoa is a clear example of the deterioration in civil and political rights in vietnam in recent months. the extensive application of national security provisions in vietnam’s penal code has resulted in a steep rise in the arrest, detention and sentencing of vietnamese citizens who peacefully express their opinions. compared to 20 years ago, reform and modernisation have allowed vietnam to make continuous progress in economic and social rights, steadily reaching out to international processes. the eu and vietnam are partners in moving from limited regional integration to meeting wider international standards. against this background, the eu is striving to reiterate, on every occasion, the concept that citizens’ opinions, expressed peacefully, enrich countries and are a pillar of sustainability and prosperity. the eu stands ready to work together with vietnam to achieve a more inclusive society.
